evidence.claim: Royal residences and temple sites line Kona’s coastal road
evidence.quote: It is a coastal road that faces the Bay of Kailua

evidence.claim: Royal residences and temple sites line Kona’s coastal road
evidence.quote: The historical sites are: Ahuena Heiau where King Kamehameha spent his retired life, the Hulihee Palace which was used by the royal family of the Hawaiian Kingdom

evidence.claim: Aliʻi Drive follows the Kailua waterfront past churches, markets, hotels and historic sites.
evidence.quote: It is a coastal road that faces the Bay of Kailua, which is home to many historical sites, resort hotels, souvenir shops, markets and churches.

evidence.claim: Royal Footsteps Along the Kona Coast covers roughly seven miles of the road.
evidence.quote: focuses on Alii Drive’s roughly seven miles of roadway

evidence.claim: Kailua Village Business Improvement District sponsored its nomination as the state’s second Hawaii Scenic Byway and presents it as a journey through seven centuries of royal archaeology, history and cultural traditions.
evidence.quote: Kailua Village Business Improvement District sponsored the nomination of Alii Drive as a Hawaii Scenic Byway. Royal Footsteps Along the Kona Coast was designated as the state’s second Hawaii Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: Kailua Village Business Improvement District sponsored its nomination as the state’s second Hawaii Scenic Byway and presents it as a journey through seven centuries of royal archaeology, history and cultural traditions.
evidence.quote: Explore seven miles and seven centuries of Hawaiian royal archaeology, history and cultural traditions.

evidence.claim: At Hōlualoa, a small beach trail became a wider highway in the nineteenth century, bisecting a royal complex.
evidence.quote: The small beach trail was widened into a larger highway later in the 19th century, bisecting the complex.

evidence.claim: Road construction changed the Kailua shore again in the 1950s, when a seawall for Aliʻi Drive destroyed much of the beach at Kamakahonu.
evidence.quote: much of the beach was destroyed to construct a seawall for Aliʻi drive in the 1950s.

evidence.claim: In 2013, the county council extended the Aliʻi Drive name south of Keauhou by renaming the adjoining Mamalahoa Bypass Road.
evidence.quote: In 2013 the Hawaii County Council changed the name of the contiguous Mamalahoa Bypass Rd. to Ali'i Drive

evidence.claim: Kamakahonu had been Kamehameha the Great’s residential compound from 1813 until his death in 1819.
evidence.quote: served as the residential compound for King Kamehameha the Great from 1813 until his death in 1819.

evidence.claim: None of its houses or walls remain; the ʻAhuʻena heiau there was reconstructed in the 1970s.
evidence.quote: none of the houses or walls remain. ʻAhuʻena heiau was reconstructed in the 1970s

evidence.claim: Begin at Kailua Pier, where the oceanfront street starts.
evidence.quote: Ali'i Drive, Kailua's oceanfront downtown street, starts at Kailua-Kona Pier.

evidence.claim: Kamakahonu lies beside the pier; Huliheʻe Palace stands on Aliʻi Drive.
evidence.quote: The Huliheʻe Palace is located in historic Kailua-Kona, Hawaiʻi, on Ali'i Drive.

evidence.claim: Kamakahonu lies beside the pier; Huliheʻe Palace stands on Aliʻi Drive.
evidence.quote: The former site of Kamakahonu Royal Center, adjacent to Kailua Pier

evidence.claim: Continuing south, Hōlualoa Bay lies between Kailua-Kona and Keauhou Bay.
evidence.quote: Hōlualoa Bay is a historic area between Kailua-Kona and Keauhou Bay

evidence.claim: Kahaluʻu Bay comes before Keauhou, where the historic shoreline includes Kamehameha III’s birthplace.
evidence.quote: Historic areas near Keauhou include Keauhou Bay, where Kamehameha III was born, Kahaluu Bay directly North

evidence.claim: Huliheʻe’s lava-rock construction acquired a new finish in 1885, when King Kalākaua had its exterior plastered.
evidence.quote: In 1885, King Kalākaua had the palace plastered over the outside

evidence.claim: Governor John Adams Kuakini originally built the palace from lava rock.
evidence.quote: The palace was originally built out of lava rock by John Adams Kuakini (governor of the island of Hawaiʻi)

evidence.claim: It later passed to Princess Ruth Keʻelikōlani, who made it her chief residence but preferred sleeping in a grass hut on the grounds.
evidence.quote: Ruth made Huliheʻe her chief residence for most of her life, but she preferred to sleep in a grass hut on the palace grounds rather than in the palace.

evidence.claim: In 1927, the Daughters of Hawaiʻi, the Territory of Hawaii and custodian Stella Maude Jones worked together to restore the palace and turn it into a museum.
evidence.quote: In 1927, the Daughters of Hawaiʻi, a group dedicated to preserving the cultural legacy of the Hawaiian Islands, working alongside the Territory of Hawaii and the palace custodian Stella Maude Jones worked to restore Huliheʻe Palace and turned it into a museum.

evidence.claim: Ruth invited reigning monarchs to vacation here, from Kamehameha III to Liliʻuokalani.
evidence.quote: She invited all of the reigning monarchs to vacation at Huliheʻe, from Kamehameha III to Liliʻuokalani.

evidence.claim: The museum displays royal furniture and artifacts.
evidence.quote: it was converted to a museum run by the Daughters of Hawaiʻi, showcasing furniture and artifacts.

evidence.claim: Aliʻi Drive divides a royal complex that developed over centuries beside Hōlualoa Bay.
evidence.quote: a large royal building complex was built over several centuries.

evidence.claim: Keākealaniwahine built a large complex here in the seventeenth century, in an area settled several hundred years earlier.
evidence.quote: Keākealaniwahine, one of the first known Aliʻi Aimoku wahine ("Queens") of the entire island of Hawaiʻi, built a large complex of buildings here in the seventeenth century, with the area settled several hundred years before that.

evidence.claim: Residential areas shared the complex with temples and burial areas.
evidence.quote: and burial areas.

evidence.claim: Residential areas shared the complex with temples and burial areas.
evidence.quote: The royal complex included residential areas, as well as Heiaus

evidence.claim: At Kamoa Point, additions included a terraced grandstand for watching surfing contests.
evidence.quote: It was added to over the years, including a terraced grandstand to watch surfing contests.

evidence.claim: The division came when the small beach trail was widened into a highway later in the nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: The small beach trail was widened into a larger highway later in the 19th century, bisecting the complex.

evidence.claim: On the north side of the bay, a nineteenth-century Christian church was restored in the 1990s and is now known as Living Stones Church.
evidence.quote:
On the north side of the bay in the 19th century, a small Christian church was built called Hale Halawai O Holualoa.
It was restored in the 1990s and now known as the "Living Stones Church".

evidence.claim: Two ancient fishponds, Waikuaʻala and Poʻo Hawaiʻi, remain visible at Kahaluʻu Bay.
evidence.quote: Two ancient fishponds called Waikuaʻala and Poʻo Hawaiʻi are still visible.

evidence.claim: The bay was an important royal residence in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
evidence.quote: in the 18th and 19th centuries was an important royal residence.

evidence.claim: At its north end, royalty used Kuʻemanu Heiau as a residence and a place to watch surfing.
evidence.quote: The Kuʻemanu Heiau is on the north end of the bay. This was used by royalty to view surfing and as a residence.

evidence.claim: South of the bay, Hāpaialiʻi Heiau was built between 1411 and 1465 and restored in 2007.
evidence.quote: South of the bay is Hāpaialiʻi Heiau, associated with astrological observation, built between 1411 and 1465 and restored in 2007.

evidence.claim: Surfers continue to use the bay, and green turtles are found in its waters.
evidence.quote: Green turtles that are still found in the bay.

evidence.claim: Surfers continue to use the bay, and green turtles are found in its waters.
evidence.quote: The bay is still used today by surfers

evidence.claim: Across Aliʻi Drive stand the stone ruins of the original Helani Church, built in 1861.
evidence.quote: Across Aliʻi Drive from the bay are the stone ruins of the original Helani Church built in 1861 by Rev. John D. Paris.

evidence.claim: Its congregation uses a later church at a higher elevation.
evidence.quote: a new Helani Church was constructed at a higher elevation still used by the congregation today.

flags: Dropped unsupported current claims: two lanes throughout, alignment with the ala loa, four of seven royal centers, palace construction in 1838, and crushed-coral mortar. The cached church source gives construction from about 1835 to 1837, not an unqualified 1835 start.
Omitted Kamehameha surfing claim: tourism source states it plainly, while the bay source says probably; neither supports the draft’s attribution to oral tradition.
Omitted the draft’s nearly enclosed breakwater claim: cache says it might have enclosed the entire bay.
Road geometry and driving time are thinly documented. Distinguish the roughly seven-mile byway from Aliʻi Drive’s later 12.5-mile extent.
No site-manager source verifies present access to individual landmarks; no opening hours or access promises included.
